Parents Are ‘Flying Blind’ in an Exploding Autism-Therapy Industry

Popular therapy known as ABA has become the default treatment for children, but quality varies and parents get little guidance

By

| Photography by Moriah Ratner for WSJ

CULPEPER, Va.—Bec and John Thompson steeled themselves as Milo thrust his little arms in their direction. “Want to hug Mommy! Want to hug Daddy!” their 4-year-old screamed.

“Don’t hug him,” Bec Thompson recalled an autism-therapy worker instructing them. “Don’t talk. Don’t respond.”

Milo banged his head on the floor in frustration and sobbed before curling up exhausted two hours later.

It was the fall of 2019. The Thompsons had turned to a widely used therapy called applied behavior analysis, or ABA, to treat Milo’s autism, which left him struggling to communicate and prone to outbursts. ABA typically uses repetition and positive reinforcement to teach desired skills and behaviors, and seeks to reduce undesired ones. The goal is to help autistic people navigate daily living.
